units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

narration_plan.release: not generated yet (generate right before publication)

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Keep a stack of the symbols still to match and look at one token: compute nullable, FIRST, and FOLLOW as least fixpoints, enter each production under the tokens that can begin it (and, when it can vanish, under the tokens that can follow it), and parse by one table lookup per expansion; a cell with two entries is the proof that the grammar is not LL(1) yet.
units.description: LL(1) parsing from a first-follow table: FIRST and FOLLOW equal the textbook sets, 13 cells, 0 conflicts; 1,500 sentences parse at 5.58 stack ops per token, recursive descent and Pratt agreeing on every tree; 1,248 corruptions rejected at the viable prefix (Earley agrees on all); the left-recursive grammar's 4 conflicts loop on 300 of 300.
units.time: O(n) stack operations, one table lookup per expansion; the table is three fixpoints over the grammar
units.space: the stack (bounded by the parse tree's frontier) plus the table
units.baseline: Hand-written recursive descent for the same grammar
units.plan_row: LL(1) parsing × First-follow table. Puzzle 203, languages-compilers (problemSlug context-free-parsing, the atlas problem page carrying "Predictive parsing"; sibling live lessons pratt-parsing-binding-powers (113) and shunting-yard-operator-stack (174)). Solution ll1_parsing_first_follow_table.py (0.2 s, prints OK): a Grammar class computing nullable, FIRST, and FOLLOW as three least fixpoints with pass counts; the LL(1) table builder recording each conflict as first/first or first/follow; a table-driven parser with an explicit stack building the parse tree and counting lookups and stack operations (with a pick rule for conflicted cells and a step cap); a seeded sentence generator; a one-token corruptor (delete, insert, swap); an Earley recognizer that also reports the longest viable prefix; a hand-written recursive descent parser counting calls; a Pratt parser whose left-associative operator tree the folded LL(1) tree must equal. ORACLES: (1) textbook expression grammar (E -> T E', E' -> + T E' | eps, T -> F T', T' -> * F T' | eps, F -> ( E ) | id): nullable {E', T'}, FIRST and FOLLOW equal Aho/Lam/Sethi/Ullman 4.4 exactly, 13 table cells, 0 conflicts, fixpoint passes 2, 4, 3; (2) 1,500 generated sentences (17,800 tokens, longest 41): all accepted, every tree re-yields its string, recursive descent agrees with 37,184 calls = the 37,184 table lookups (one per expansion), the folded tree equals the Pratt tree on all 1,500; (3) 1,500 corruptions: 1,248 rejected, Earley agrees on all 1,500 and recursive descent too, every LL(1) error position equals the longest viable prefix (correct-prefix property); (4) work: stack ops = 5.58 x tokens + 9.0, every parse within 16 ops of the line, max 14 ops per token (one-token input), asserted under 20 residual and under 15 per token; Earley 78,715 chart items (4.4 per token) and 3x the LL(1) time on the corruptions; (5) left-recursive grammar E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F: 4 FIRST/FIRST conflicts (E and T on id and '('); the transformed grammar agrees with Earley on the original on 1,200 strings both ways; fed directly, preferring the recursive production loops (step cap) on 300 of 300 valid inputs, preferring the other rejects 252 of 300 (every input containing + or *); (6) dangling else S -> if c then S S' | other, S' -> else S | eps: exactly 1 FIRST/FOLLOW conflict on (S', else); preferring 'else S' binds the else to the innermost if at depths 1 to 6 on 6 nestings, preferring eps rejects all 6; S -> a b | a c: 1 conflict, left-factored 0. AUTHOR CORRECTION recorded in the header: the draft asserted every parse within three slopes of the linear fit; one-token inputs sit 16 ops off the line, so the page states the measured bound. Cards: self (algoName LL(1) parsing), Recursive descent parsing, LALR parsing x Merged lookahead states, Pratt parsing x Binding-power dispatch (live lesson badge); all pages exist in dist/algo. neverUse: the left-recursive grammar fed straight to the LL(1) parser (4 conflicts; loops on 300 of 300 or rejects 252 of 300). Contest: conflicts / valid accepted / corruptions rejected / work per token for the LL(1) table, recursive descent (2.09 calls per token), Earley (4.4 items, 3x time), and LL(1) on the left-recursive grammar. Figure: nullable/FIRST/FOLLOW table beside the 5 x 6 parse table with its 13 filled cells; cites Lewis and Stearns 1968 (DOI 10.1145/321466.321477), Knuth 1971 (DOI 10.1007/BF00289517), Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman 4.4. Viz Ll1ParsingViz: a table-driven parse of a seeded 3-to-14-token expression (35% carry a one-token corruption), one parser step per tick, the input row with consumed and lookahead tokens, the stack, the 5 x 6 table with the active cell lit, counters of steps, lookups, and expansions; invariant: lookups equal expansions and the verdict equals an independent recursive descent recognizer; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 420, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Take any edge with neither end chosen, put both ends in the cover, delete what they touch, repeat: the kept edges are a maximal matching, every cover needs one vertex per kept edge, so the output is at most twice the optimum in one linear pass, with the matching as a receipt; the max-degree greedy beats it on average and loses by a logarithm when the graph is chosen against it.
units.description: The maximal-matching rule against exact optima on 300 random graphs: 1.495 × OPT mean, 2.000 worst, |M| ≤ OPT ≤ 2|M| on every graph; K6,6 and a star return exactly 2 × OPT; the max-degree greedy averages 1.032 but climbs 2.125, 2.719, 3.375, 4.039 on the bad family at n = 16 to 128 (OPT by Kőnig) while the matching rule stays at 2.000.
units.time: O(V + E): one pass over the edges
units.space: O(V) for the cover and the matching
units.baseline: Max-degree greedy (greedy set cover on edges)
units.plan_row: Greedy vertex cover × Maximal matching. Puzzle 204, optimization-or (problemSlug vertex-cover, the atlas problem page carrying "Vertex cover 2-approximation"; sibling live lessons greedy-set-cover-max-coverage, branchbound-fractional, hopcroft-karp-layered-phases). Solution greedy_vertex_cover_maximal_matching.py (1.0 s, prints OK): the matching rule, the max-degree greedy with incremental degrees, exact branch and bound (branch on the max-degree vertex, prune with the matching bound), brute force for small graphs, Kuhn's augmenting-path matching, Konig's cover from the matching, the half-integral LP solved through the bipartite double cover with a dual fractional matching as the optimality certificate, and the generator for the degree greedy's bad family. ORACLES: (1) exact solver equals brute force on 60 graphs of 6 to 11 vertices; (2) 300 random G(14, 0.3) graphs: matching rule 1.495 mean / 2.000 worst against OPT (15 branch-and-bound nodes mean), |M| <= OPT <= 2|M| and a valid cover on every graph; degree greedy 1.032 / 1.286; LP rounding at one half 1.757 / 2.000; OPT/LP 1.123 mean; primal feasible, dual feasible, values equal on every graph; (3) edge order: one order 1.491 against best of eight shuffles 1.289 (40 graphs); (4) tight examples: K6,6 cover 12 against OPT 6 (ratio 2.0, degree greedy optimal at 6), star K1,8 cover 2 against 1; (5) Konig: min cover = max matching = brute force on 40 random bipartite graphs; (6) bad family (n left vertices; for each i in 2..n, n // i right vertices of degree i): OPT = n exactly by Konig; degree greedy takes every right vertex, 34 / 87 / 216 / 517 at n = 16 / 32 / 64 / 128, ratios 2.125 / 2.719 / 3.375 / 4.039 against H_n - 1 = 4.433 at 128; matching rule 2.000 on each; (7) exact search at average degree 4: 24 / 118 / 919 / 4,514 / 31,496 nodes at n = 24 / 48 / 72 / 96 / 120 (asserted > 100x growth). Two author corrections recorded in the header: the draft guessed the matching rule's worst case over random graphs at 1.90 and measured exactly 2.00; the draft expected branch and bound to blow up by n = 24 on dense random graphs, where the matching bound prunes to a few dozen nodes, so the growth experiment moved to sparse graphs. Cards: self, LP rounding vertex cover (algoName), Greedy set cover (max-degree greedy, live lesson badge), Branch and bound (live lesson badge). neverUse: the max-degree greedy when the graph may be chosen against you (the bad family ratios). Figure: mean and worst ratios for three methods beside the bad-family ratio climbing with n against the matching rule's flat 2.000; cite Gavril in Garey and Johnson 1979, Karp 1972, Khot and Regev 2008 (DOI 10.1016/j.jcss.2007.06.019), Konig 1931. Viz VertexCoverViz: a seeded random graph of 11 to 14 vertices on a circle, one edge per tick, amber kept edges and blue cover vertices, deleted edges faded, the exact optimum by brute force over subsets, invariant that deleted edges touch the cover and |cover| = 2|M|, final check |M| <= OPT <= 2|M| and every edge covered; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 420, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Treat roads as hidden states and GPS fixes as noisy observations, score each fix by its distance to a road and each hop by how far the driving distance strays from the straight line, and let Viterbi pick the most probable route: 95.6% of fixes on the true segment with half a percent of route-length error where nearest-road snapping manages 90.6% and a 47% detour.
units.description: Hidden Markov map matching (Newson and Krumm 2009) against an exhaustive optimum and the hidden route: Viterbi equals the brute-force maximum on 40 traces (339,964 sequences); 95.6% of fixes on the true segment at 4 m noise against 90.6% for snapping, route-length error 0.5% against 46.6%; the frontage road took 83 of 800 snapped fixes, 1 matched.
units.time: O(T C^2) transitions after one Dijkstra per intersection
units.space: O(V^2) route table plus O(T C) lattice
units.plan_row: Hidden Markov map matching × Emission-transition road probabilities. Puzzle 205, geometry (problemSlug map-matching, the atlas problem page carrying "Map matching"; sibling live lessons viterbi-max-product, puzzle 29, and monte-carlo-localization-particle-filter, puzzle 138). Solution hidden_markov_map_matching_emission_transition_road_probabilities.py (0.7 s, prints OK): a synthetic city of 75 intersections and 132 segments (a 9 x 7 grid of avenues 100 m apart, 8 diagonals, two frontage roads 18 m beside an avenue joined only at their ends), a 75 x 75 route table from 75 Dijkstra runs (19,800 relaxations), hidden simple-path routes, fixes every 35 m with Gaussian noise, candidates within 25 + 3 sigma m, emission -(d/sigma)^2/2, transition -|straight-line - route|/beta with beta fitted Newson-Krumm style as the median gap / ln 2 on 10 known-truth traces per noise level (6.02, 10.36, 15.31, 23.16 m at sigma 4, 8, 12, 20). ORACLES: (a) Viterbi equals the exhaustive maximum over every candidate sequence on 40 short traces (339,964 sequences enumerated) to 1e-9, and its score equals its own terms re-summed; (b) against the hidden route, 20 traces per sigma: on the true segment HMM 0.956 / 0.886 / 0.827 / 0.703 vs snapping 0.906 / 0.800 / 0.706 / 0.597; position error 3.3 / 6.6 / 10.3 / 18.3 m vs 3.5 / 7.5 / 12.2 / 21.2; route-length error 0.005 / 0.026 / 0.074 / 0.290 vs 0.466 / 0.807 / 1.052 / 1.203; candidates per fix 3.74 / 4.66 / 5.56 / 8.12; (c) beta = infinity reproduces nearest-road snapping on every fix; along the 600 m avenue at sigma 10 the frontage road took 83 of 800 snapped fixes (10.4%) and 1 matched fix; (d) thinning at sigma 8: every fix 0.894 vs 0.814, every 2nd 0.902 vs 0.831, every 4th 0.864 vs 0.809; (e) one 39-fix trace: 164 candidates, 749 lattice edges against 1.63e23 sequences. Three author corrections recorded (frontage capture 10.4% not a fifth, cross streets take fixes; thinning by two cost nothing; snapping's position error only slightly worse, the gap is the route). Cards: self, Viterbi algorithm (live lesson), ST-Matching, Particle filter (live lesson) (all algoName). neverUse: nearest-road snapping for a route. Figure: the avenue with its frontage road, fixes, red snapping flips against the matched route, beside route-length error bars at four noise levels; cite Newson and Krumm 2009 (DOI 10.1145/1653771.1653818), Viterbi 1967, Quddus, Ochieng, Noland 2007. Viz MapMatchingViz: a seeded 7 x 4 road grid with a frontage road, a hidden route (the avenue past the frontage road or a random path), fixes revealed one per tick, Viterbi and snapping re-run on the prefix each tick, the invariant that the Viterbi path equals the exhaustive maximum on short prefixes (or beats every one-candidate change on long ones) and beats the snapping path; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 380, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Scan from the right for the longest non-increasing suffix, swap the element before it with the rightmost suffix element larger than it, reverse the suffix: Narayana's fourteenth-century rule visits every arrangement of a multiset exactly once in dictionary order, in place with two indices, at a constant amortized cost per step (mean suffix e - 1), where the single-swap orders of Heap and Johnson-Trotter are cheaper per step and unsorted.
units.description: Algorithm L against itertools for every n to 8 and the multinomial on MISSISSIPPI (34,650): all 362,880 arrangements of nine in 0.12 s with a mean suffix of 1.718 = e − 1 and 1.54 swaps per step; Heap and Johnson-Trotter use 5,039 single swaps but break sorted order 2,513 and 2,519 times; Lehmer unranking matches on 2,000 ranks.
units.time: O(1) amortized per arrangement (mean suffix e − 1); O(n) for one worst step
units.space: O(1) extra: two indices, in place
units.baseline: Heap's algorithm (one swap per arrangement, unsorted)
units.plan_row: Lexicographic permutations × Next-permutation algorithm. Puzzle 206, dp-combinatorics (problemSlug permutation-generation, the atlas problem page carrying "Permutation generation"; sibling live lessons fisher-yates-uniform-swaps (puzzle 46) and held-karp-bitmask-states (puzzle 81)). Solution lexicographic_permutations_next_permutation_algorithm.py (1.6 s, prints OK, 21 checks): Algorithm L with counters for comparisons, swaps, moves, and suffix length; a lexicographic enumerator; Heap's algorithm (iterative); Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter with Even's directions; Lehmer rank and unrank; a copying recursion; next bigger number by rule and by brute force. ORACLES: (1) the rule equals itertools.permutations for n = 1 to 8 (40,320 at n = 8), each arrangement strictly greater than the last; (2) multisets [0,0,1,1,2], [0,0,0,1,1,2,2], MISSISSIPPI (34,650), [1,1,1,1] each listed once, equal to sorted(set(permutations)) and the multinomial; (3) over the full enumeration at n = 8 and 9: mean suffix 1.718 (asserted within 0.01 of e − 1 = 1.718), comparisons 3.077, swaps 1.543 (asserted in 1.50 to 1.60), moves 3.086 per step; n = 9 (362,880) in 0.12 s; (4) Heap's algorithm at n = 7: 5,040 arrangements each once, 5,039 swaps, 2,513 descents, sorted set equal to the lexicographic list; Johnson-Trotter: 5,040 once, 5,039 swaps each of two adjacent positions, 2,519 descents; Algorithm L 0 descents; (5) unrank(k, 8) equals the k-th sequential arrangement and rank inverts it on 2,000 random k plus k = 0, 1, 40,319; (6) 12! = 479,001,600 would take about 3 minutes and 20! = 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 about 26,240 years at the measured n = 9 pace (honest extrapolation); (7) the copying recursion copies 38.7 elements per arrangement at n = 8 and produces the same set; (8) next bigger number with the same digits agrees with brute force on 300 random digit strings of length 4 to 7, 52 with no answer. AUTHOR CORRECTION recorded in the header: the draft guessed 1.36 swaps per step; the measurement is 1.543 because reversing a suffix of length L costs floor(L/2) swaps, mean 0.543 under the 1/k! suffix law; and Heap's one swap per step is cheaper per step but buys no order, which the page states instead. Cards: self, Heap's algorithm, Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Factorial number system × Lehmer code ranking (all algoName pages present). neverUse: regenerating the whole census for one next-arrangement question (40,320 strings for an eight-digit number; 38.7 copies per arrangement). Figure: one step on 1 2 5 4 3 (pivot 2, partner 3, swap, reverse) beside bars of the per-step costs and the descents of the three orders; cite Knuth TAOCP 4A 7.2.1.2 Algorithm L, Narayana Pandita 1356, Sedgewick 1977 (DOI 10.1145/356689.356692). Viz NextPermutationViz: a seeded multiset of five letters, one arrangement per tick with pivot and partner in amber and the reversed suffix in blue, a progress bar against the multinomial count, invariant that each arrangement is greater than the last and uses the same letters and that the final count equals the multinomial; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 28.75 ticks per cycle, 0 breaks; stepMs 170, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Keep one running level and move it a fraction alpha toward each observation: the forecast is the level, and the recursion is a weighted average of the whole past with weights alpha (1 - alpha)^k that fade geometrically, sum to one, and sit (1 - alpha)/alpha values back on average; fit alpha by squared one-step error and it lands on the Kalman gain.
units.description: Exponential smoothing: the recursion equals the unrolled geometric sum to 3e-14; the fitted alpha 0.390 +- 0.003 lands on the Kalman gain 0.390 over 150 series; one-step RMSE 1.284 against a floor of 1.281, moving average 1.321, naive 1.499, mean 4.662; a trend lags by b/alpha (0.96); a season trails by a month, 7.86 against 2.84.
units.plan_row: Exponential smoothing × Geometric decay weights. Puzzle 207, ml-ai (problemSlug time-series-forecasting, the atlas problem page carrying "Short-term forecasting"; sibling live lessons holt-winters-triple-seasonal-smoothing, puzzle 164, and kalman-covariance-correction, puzzle 97). Solution exponential_smoothing_geometric_decay_weights.py (1.2 s, prints OK): the smoothing recursion, the unrolled geometric sum, a coarse-grid plus golden-section fitter on one-step squared error, a local level simulator, the ARIMA(0,1,1) recursion, Holt's linear trend with a grid fit, a moving average, and a compact additive Holt-Winters. ORACLES: (1) recursion = unrolled sum to 2.8e-14 on random series at alpha 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8; weights at alpha 0.3 sum to 1.000000000000 with mean lag 2.3333 = (1 - a)/a, half the weight inside the last 2 values; (2) local level model q = 0.25: Kalman gain 0.3904, squared-error fit over 150 series of 400: 0.3899 +- 0.0035; ARIMA(0,1,1) with theta -0.6096 forecasts equal to 2.8e-14; (3) one-step RMSE, fitted on the first half and scored on the second half of 150 series: smoothing 1.284 +- 0.005 (MAE 1.026), innovation floor 1.281, moving average 1.321 +- 0.007 (MAE 1.057, best window 4.2 on average), naive 1.499 +- 0.007 (MAE 1.199), mean 4.662 +- 0.176, alpha 0.01: 3.498 +- 0.103; (4) trend b = 0.5 with noise 2 over 60 series: fitted alpha 0.52, one-step lag 0.960 +- 0.008 against b/alpha 0.959, RMSE 2.523; Holt bias -0.001 +- 0.005, RMSE 2.246; (5) h-step intervals over 400 series at the Kalman gain with sigma estimated in-sample: coverage 0.925 (h=1), 0.945 (h=2), 0.935 (h=5), 0.935 (h=10); error variance ratio at h=10 2.35 against 1 + 9 alpha^2 = 2.37; (6) seasonal wave (amplitude 20, noise 2, 40 series): smoothing 7.86 trailing the signal by 1.0 months, seasonal naive 2.84, Holt-Winters (alpha 0.2, gamma 0.3) 2.29. Two author corrections recorded (the trend lag is b/alpha, not b(1 - alpha)/alpha; measured coverage 0.925 to 0.945, not 0.95, so the assertion is a 0.92 to 0.98 band). Cards: self, Moving average × Sliding window, Holt linear trend × Level plus trend smoothing, ARIMA × Box-Jenkins identification (all algoName pages present). neverUse: simple smoothing on a seasonal series (7.86 against 2.84 and 2.29, trailing by a month). Figure: the geometric weights for alpha 0.3 and 0.1 beside log-scale one-step RMSE bars for six methods; cite Brown 1956, Holt 1957 / 2004 (DOI 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2003.09.015), Hyndman, Koehler, Ord, Snyder 2008. Viz ExponentialSmoothingViz: a seeded local level series, one value per tick, the level at the Kalman gain of the drawn q, the geometric weights drawn under the cursor, running one-step RMSE for smoothing, a four-value moving average, and the naive forecast; invariant: the recursive level equals the unrolled sum to 1e-9; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 119 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 110, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Train on what is labeled, score the pool, and buy the label of the one point whose top class the model is least sure of, the point nearest its boundary: three labels saved in four on a four-dimensional boundary, one scoring pass per round, and a blind spot the size of everything the model is confidently wrong about.
units.description: Pool-based active learning with a Newton-trained logistic regression against random sampling, 30 seeds: 13 labels against 44 to reach 0.903 in four dimensions (AULC 0.9072 vs 0.8759, 4.1 standard errors), 2.7 in the plane, none with a wide gap; a hidden cluster got 0 of 40 queries and 0.000 accuracy where random reached 0.838.
units.time: O(|pool| x d) scoring plus one model fit per query
units.space: O(|pool| x d) for the pool and the model
units.baseline: Random sampling from the same pool
units.plan_row: Uncertainty sampling × Least-confidence query. Puzzle 208, ml-ai (problemSlug active-learning, the atlas problem page carrying "Active learning"; sibling live lessons perceptron-mistake-driven-updates, puzzle 130, and thompson-sampling-posterior-draws, puzzle 109). Solution uncertainty_sampling_least_confidence_query.py (7.0 s, prints OK): a Newton-trained L2 logistic regression with a small Gaussian elimination, a pool-based active learning loop taking a strategy, a seed set, and an optional density weight, a softmax regression for three classes, a farthest-first traversal for diversity seeds, and a Gaussian kernel density over the pool. units.oneLiner: Sort the jobs longest first and hand each to the machine that is least loaded so far: the long jobs settle while the machines are empty and the short ones level the ends, so the makespan is never worse than 4/3 - 1/(3m) times the optimum (Graham 1969, tight), against 2 - 1/m for the same rule in arrival order; one sort, one pass, and a lower bound as the receipt.
units.description: Graham's LPT rule against exact optima on 300 random instances: 1.0212 × OPT mean, 1.1739 worst, inside 4/3 − 1/(3m); arrival order 1.1221 and 1.4688; the tight families hit 7/6, 11/9, 15/12, 19/15 and 2 − 1/m exactly; MULTIFIT wins 148, ties 100, loses 52; LPT met the lower bound on 20 of 20 thousand-job instances.
units.time: O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log m) placements
units.space: O(m) machine loads plus the sorted order

Solution job_scheduling_approximation_longest_processing_time.py (0.2 s, prints OK): list scheduling to the least loaded machine, the LPT wrapper, the lower bound max(p, ceil(sum/m)), branch and bound on jobs sorted longest first (one machine tried per distinct load, pruned by the remaining work and by min load + next job), brute force over all m^n assignments, first fit decreasing with a capacity search (MULTIFIT), a move-or-swap local search from the LPT schedule, and the two tight-family generators. ORACLES: (1) exact solver equals brute force on 60 instances of 4 to 8 jobs on 2 or 3 machines; (2) 300 random instances (n = 10..14, m = 2..4, sizes 1..50): LPT/OPT mean 1.0212, worst 1.1739, optimal on 75 of 300, worst by machine count 1.0526 / 1.1111 / 1.1739 against the bounds 1.1667 / 1.2222 / 1.2500; arrival order mean 1.1221, worst 1.4688 (bound 2 - 1/m); MULTIFIT mean 1.0099, worst 1.0833, against LPT wins 148, ties 100, losses 52; local search from LPT mean 1.0045, worst 1.0566, never above LPT; exact search 310 nodes mean, lower bound equal to OPT on 240 of 300; (3) tight families: LPT returns 4m - 1 against OPT 3m, 7/6, 11/9, 15/12, 19/15 for m = 2 to 5 (4/3 - 1/(3m) exactly); the arrival-order family (m(m-1) unit jobs then one job of length m) returns 2m - 1 against m, LPT optimal there; (4) 20 instances of n = 1,000 on m = 10 (sizes 1..100): LPT met the lower bound on 20 of 20, MULTIFIT never below it, arrival order 0.87% above on average and 1.11% at most; (5) adversarial order at m = 10: list 19 against OPT 10 (ratio 1.90), LPT 10; (6) exact search at m = 3 with sizes 1..1000: 988 / 4,795 / 54,121 / 27,022 nodes at n = 12 / 16 / 20 / 24 (asserted more than tenfold growth). Two author corrections recorded in the header: the draft expected LPT about 10 percent above the optimum on small random instances (measured 2 percent), and expected MULTIFIT to tie LPT on most instances (it won about half).
